title: Karoo Precision

sentences.text: Karoo Precision Ltd (Karoo) is a JSE-listed industrial manufacturer whose share price dropped 35% this year
ahead of a planned rights issue to raise emergency capital.
After reporting its third consecutive annual operating loss and negative operating cash flows for the year ended 30 June 2026,
Karoo breached the interest-cover covenant on its R400 million long-term bank loan, with no lender waiver obtained by year-end.
Operations are further strained because 60% of Karoo’s raw materials are imported in US dollars on unhedged terms during a period of sharp rand depreciation.
Shortly after year-end, Karoo’s largest customer (accounting for 30% of revenue and owing R45 million) entered business rescue,
while a key supplier sued Karoo for R30 million over cancelled supply contracts.
To cut costs, the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) retrenched two senior financial accountants mid-year
and now personally processes manual year-end journals.
Although Karoo’s independent Audit Committee appointed your firm as new external auditors for FY2026 to improve reporting credibility,
and its largest institutional shareholder has signed a non-binding letter of comfort,
the board has already drafted the annual financial statements on the going concern basis.

required: Assess the risk of material misstatement at the financial statement level of Karoo Precision Ltd for the FY2026 audit. One of the 12 marks is for communication: clarity of expression.

recall.question: What kind of business is Karoo?
options: A JSE-listed industrial manufacturer
An unlisted family-owned retailer
A bank that lends to manufacturers
An importer and distributor of US goods

recall.question: What is your role?
options: The external auditor, in your firm's first year on the audit
The external auditor, several years into the audit
The internal auditor reporting to the Audit Committee
The CFO preparing the annual financial statements

recall.question: What is Karoo's main problem this year?
options: Financial distress: losses, a broken loan covenant and a need for emergency capital
Fast growth that the finance team cannot keep up with
A planned listing on the JSE
A tax dispute with SARS

recall.question: On what basis has the board drafted the financial statements?
options: The going concern basis
A liquidation basis
IFRS for SMEs
They have not been drafted yet
An assessment: the factors that increase the risk, the factors that reduce it, and a conclusion on the overall level
A list of the risks only
A list of audit procedures to respond to each risk
A calculation of planning materiality
shape.why: “Assess” needs both sides and a conclusion. The mark plan gives marks for the two factors that reduce the risk and one for concluding that the risk is high. A list of risks only stops short.

options.text: Stay at the financial statement level: risks that affect the statements as a whole
One mark is for communication: clarity of expression
Give audit procedures for each risk
Recommend whether your firm should accept the engagement

directions.why: The level is the big one: financial statement level means risks that spread across the statements (pressure, incentives, weak controls, going concern, big judgements). Audit procedures are a different required and earn nothing here.

options: The external auditor: how each fact could cause a material misstatement in Karoo’s financial statements
The board: how to fix Karoo’s business problems
The bank: whether to call up the loan
An investor: whether to take up the rights issue
lens.why: Every point has to end in the financial statements: who might manipulate them, what could be wrong in them. “The business is struggling” is business risk; it earns the mark only once you say what it does to the statements.

rows.point: Listed, share price down 35%: pressure on management to manipulate the financial statements to meet market and shareholder expectations
Planned rights issue for emergency capital: incentive to overstate assets and income, and understate liabilities and expenses, so Karoo looks like an attractive investment
Covenant breach, no waiver: incentive to manipulate profit or interest cover to hide or cure the breach, so the R400 million loan is not called up
Covenant breach, no waiver at year-end: risk the R400 million loan is classified as non-current instead of current (IAS 1), and the default is not adequately disclosed
rows.why: The case gives the breach and the missing waiver. Apply IAS 1: no waiver by year-end means no right to defer settlement, so the loan is current.

rows.point: Two senior financial accountants retrenched mid-year: understaffed finance function, weak review, higher risk of error across the statements
CFO personally processes manual year-end journals: no segregation of duties, opportunity for management override and fraudulent reporting
First-year audit for your firm: risk that opening balances are materially misstated
rows.why: The case only says your firm is new. The step: a first audit means nobody in your firm audited last year's closing balances, which are this year's opening balances.

rows.point: First-year audit for your firm: risk that accounting policies are not applied consistently with prior years
rows.why: Same clue, a second step: a new auditor has not seen how the policies were applied before.

rows.point: Risk that the going concern basis is inappropriate, or that a material uncertainty is not (adequately) disclosed in terms of IAS 1
rows.why: The case says the board used the going concern basis. You draw the conclusion: with these indicators, that basis, or the missing disclosure, is itself a risk of material misstatement.

rows.point: Going concern indicator: third consecutive operating loss and negative operating cash flows, sustained decline and cash burn
Going concern indicator: no waiver means the R400 million loan is repayable on demand, acute liquidity strain
Going concern indicator: 60% unhedged US dollar imports while the rand depreciates squeeze margins and cash flows
rows.why: The case gives unhedged dollar imports and a weak rand. The step: a weaker rand makes every import cost more, with nothing in place to protect Karoo.

rows.point: Going concern indicator: largest customer (30% of revenue) in business rescue and the R30 million supplier lawsuit threaten future revenue and cash
IAS 36: recurring losses and the 35% share price drop are impairment indicators; value in use estimates are subjective and open to bias to avoid impairment
rows.why: The case gives losses and a falling share price. Apply IAS 36: these are indicators of impairment, which brings in subjective estimates.

rows.point: IAS 21 / IAS 2: unhedged dollar imports bring translation errors (spot rate, closing-rate retranslation of payables) and possible inventory write-downs to net realisable value
rows.why: The case gives dollar imports on unhedged terms. Apply IAS 21 and IAS 2 to see where the numbers can go wrong.

rows.point: IAS 10 / IFRS 9 / IAS 37: judgement on the post year-end business rescue (R45 million receivable, expected credit losses) and the R30 million lawsuit (provision or contingent liability)
rows.why: The case gives two events after year-end. Apply IAS 10, IFRS 9 and IAS 37 to decide whether they adjust the figures, and how.

rows.point: Reduces the risk: an independent Audit Committee appointing new auditors to improve reporting credibility shows active governance oversight
rows.why: The case even signals it with “Although”. Assess needs both sides, so the factors that reduce the risk earn marks too.

rows.point: Reduces the risk, but only partly: the shareholder’s letter of comfort supports going concern, but it is non-binding, so the uncertainty remains
Conclusion: the incentives, weak controls, complex judgements and going concern indicators outweigh the mitigating factors, so the risk at the financial statement level is high
Communication: clear, plain language, so the reader can follow each risk from the case fact to its effect on the financial statements
rows.why: Communication is judged across the whole answer, not on one fact in the case.
